<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par123 />{{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=10|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=26|verse=13}} and often (cf. Cheyne, ''Bampton Lectures'', 1889, p. 479, according to whom the use of the {{GHGheb|text=ו}} copulative with the second word is especially common in Ch and Est, and therefore belongs to the later language; Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}<sup>6</sup>, p. 538, No. 35); sometimes (but with the exception of {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=18}} only in very late passages) with a pleonastic {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} preceding, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=145|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=2|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Est|chapter=9|verse=28|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=11|verse=12}}, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|123|d}}
2. Repetition of words in an expressly ''distributive'' sense<ref>Cf. in the New Testament {{GHGbible-ref|book=St. Mark|chapter=6|verse=39}} f. συμπόσια συμπόσια, πρασιαὶ πρασιαί (Weizsäcker, ''tischweise, beetweise'').</ref> (which may to some extent be noticed in the examples under c) equivalent to ''one each'', &c., e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=34}} ''forty days'' {{GHGheb|text=יוֹם לַשָּׁנָה יוֹם לַשָּׁנָה|translate=counting for every day a year}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=24|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=28|verse=34}} (three words repeated); also with the addition of {{GHGheb|text=לְבַד|translate=apart}}, {{GHGheb|text=עֵדֶר עֵדֶר לְבַדּוֹ|translate=every drove by itself}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=32|verse=17}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=12|verse=12}}. Most frequently with the addition of a numeral (for the simple repetition of numerals for the same purpose, cf. {{GHGpar|134|q}}), and with the words not only in groups of two ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=24|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=13|verse=2}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=31|verse=4|hidebook=1}}) or three ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=7|verse=11}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=17|verse=21|hidebook=1}}), but even of six ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=26|verse=3}}) or seven ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=25|verse=33}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=26|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, 21, 25); in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=25|verse=35}} five words even three times repeated.<ref>These repetitions of larger groups of words belong entirely to the ''Priestly Code'' in the Pentateuch, and are unquestionably indications of a late period of the language. Of quite a different kind are such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ez|chapter=16|verse=6}}, where the repetition of four words serves to give greater solemnity to the promise, unless here, as certainly in 1:20, it is a mere ''dittography''; the LXX omit the repetition, in both passages.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|123|e}}
3. Repetition to express an exceptional or at least superfine quality; e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=15}} ''which were of gold, gold, of silver, silver'', i.e. made of pure gold and pure silver; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=2|verse=27}} {{GHGheb|text=בַּדֶּ֫רֶךְ בַּדֶּ֫רֶךְ|translate=only along by the}} high ''way''; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=8|verse=16|hidebook=1}} ''they are given, given to him'', i.e. given exclusively for his service, for his very own. Also with a certain hyperbole in such examples as {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=16}} {{GHGheb|text=גֵּבִים גֵּבִים|translate=nothing but trenches}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=14|verse=10}} {{GHGheb|text=בֶּֽאֱרֹת בֶּֽאֱרֹת חֵמָר|translate=all asphalt-pits}}.—Repetition serves to intensify the expression to the highest degree in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=5|verse=22}} ''by reason of the violent pransings of his string ones'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=8|verse=10}} (''countless heaps''), and {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jo|chapter=4|verse=14}} (''countless multitudes''); cf. also {{GHGheb|text=מְעַט מְעַט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=23|verse=30}} ''by little and little, very gradually''; cf. {{GHGpar|133|k}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|123|f}}
4. Repetition with the copula to express ''of more than one kind''; thus {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=25|verse=13}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=20|verse=10}}) {{GHGheb|text=אֶ֫בֶן וָאֶ֫בֶן|translate=a weight and a weight}}, i.e. two kinds of weight (hence the addition ''great and small''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=12|verse=3}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּלֵב וָלֵב|translate=with two kinds of heart}}, i.e. ''with a double-dealing heart''; cf. the opposite {{GHGheb|text=בְּלֹא לֵב וָלֵב}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=12|verse=33}}.<section end=par123 />

<section begin=par124 />{{GHGpar-heading|124|The Various Uses of the Plural-form||<ref>Cf. Dietrich, ‘''Über Begriff und Form des hebr. Plurals'',’ in the {{GHGcite|title=Abhandl. zur hebr. Grammatik}}, Leipzig, 1846, p. 2 ff.</ref>}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|124|a}}
'''1.''' The plural is by no means used in Hebrew solely to express a number of individuals or separate objects, but may also denote them collectively. This use of the plural expresses either (''a'') a combination of various external constituent parts (plurals of ''local extension''), or (''b'') a more or less intensive focusing of the characteristics inherent in the idea of the stem (''abstract plurals'', usually rendered in English by forms in ''-hood, -ness, -ship'').
